title: 2026 U.S. Senate elections
text:
Silicon sampling asks large language models to play survey respondents (Argyle et al. 2023). Each synthetic voter is a persona built from a real respondent of the 2024 Cooperative Election Study (CES): age, gender, race, education, income, party identification, ideology and so on. We describe the persona to a model, tell it the 2026 Senate race in the persona’s state, and ask how the persona will vote. Many personas, several models and five repeats each give a synthetic electorate, which is weighted to the real one. Synthetic samples can be biased in ways real polls are not (Bisbee et al. 2024), so a 2024 backtest against the real results is used to calibrate every forecast below.
This is the project’s main approach. The conventional regression forecast follows in the second part of this page.






NoteReal LLM results



Everything in this part comes from stored model replies (5,173 personas in 35 states, three models) collected on 30 to 31 October 2026 and processed by scripts/04-forecast.py; this page re-reads the saved files and queries no model.

Composition of the 2026 persona sample.




Personas are real 2024 CES respondents (scripts/02-build_personas.py), at most 150 per state, written up in the first person. The sample is built from 2024 respondents even for 2026, so it describes the 2024 electorate, not 2026 voters.



Each reply is one call to a model with this system prompt and persona-plus-question prompt (an illustration; no model is called here):
You will be given a description of a person. Answer from this person's perspective, using only knowledge about politics that they would have.

I am a 67-year-old Hispanic woman living in Texas. I have some college education but no degree. My family income is between $80,000 and $100,000 a year. In politics, I consider myself a strong Democrat. I would describe my political views as moderate. I never attend religious services. I follow what's going on in government and public affairs hardly at all.

It is November 2026. In this year's midterm U.S. Senate election in Texas, the main candidates are a Republican and a Democrat. I will vote for ...

Reply with exactly one of: Republican, Democrat, Other, Would not vote. No other text.
The wording follows Bisbee et al. (2024): answer as the person, using only what they would know. Every persona is asked five times per model at temperature 1.0, so a persona’s answer is a distribution, not a single vote. Pure independents mostly answer “Other”, so they are asked a second, forced-choice question that allows only the Republican or the main opponent, as in survey follow-ups for undecided voters.




Persona share. For each persona and model, the Republican share is Republican answers divided by answers for any major candidate actually on the ballot (Republican, Democrat or independent). Pure independents use their forced-choice answers.
Weights. Each persona counts as its CES survey weight times its chance of voting: validated turnout for 2024, and turnout rates by age group, college and news interest estimated from CES 2022 for the 2026 midterm.
State estimate. The weighted mean of persona shares, with a bootstrap standard error.




Raw synthetic shares are not forecasts. For each backtested model a line is fitted to the 33 races of 2024 (GPT-4o mini: actual = 0.19 + 0.65 × estimate; Llama 3.3 70B: actual = 0.21 + 0.62 × estimate), which pulls the estimates toward the middle and shifts them toward Republicans. The 2026 estimates are passed through that line. Uncertainty then comes from five sources in 10,000 simulated elections: a national swing shared by all states (standard deviation 3 points, an assumption, because one election cannot measure it), a state-level error (standard deviation 4.7 points, measured by leaving each 2024 race out in turn), the model used, and sampling error in the synthetic voters.

Person by person, the synthetic voters agree with the real vote 91% of the time, slightly below a party-line baseline that simply has everyone vote with their side (95%); that baseline cannot predict independents, who are where the models help and where they are weakest. At the state level the raw estimates are too Democratic (the bias column) and too spread out (calibration slopes near 0.6), which is why calibration is needed. After it, the models still miss by about six points on average and call 28 of 33 winners.

Silicon sampling is calibrated on a single election (2024), while the regression is validated against certified results from six cycles; the second part of this page documents the regression and its accuracy.




Synthetic is not a poll. The “voters” are 2024 respondents described to a model; no one answered a 2026 survey.
Calibration rests on one election. The line that corrects the models is fitted to 33 races in 2024, and a midterm may differ.
Some uncertainty is assumed, not measured. The 3-point national swing is a judgement, and the seats-not-up count is taken from the forecast script.
Candidates are described by party, not name. The model cannot know who the nominees are, so the favoured candidate is the nominee of the favoured side.
Independents are the hard part. Models agree with real independents about two thirds of the time in 2024, and four races have an independent challenger.
Models differ in knowledge. The backtested models have older knowledge cutoffs than DeepSeek V4 Flash, which has no backtest.

title: 2026 U.S. Senate elections
text:
Composition of the 2026 persona sample.




Personas are real 2024 CES respondents (scripts/02-build_personas.py), at most 150 per state, written up in the first person. The sample is built from 2024 respondents even for 2026, so it describes the 2024 electorate, not 2026 voters.



Each reply is one call to a model with this system prompt and persona-plus-question prompt (an illustration; no model is called here):
You will be given a description of a person. Answer from this person's perspective, using only knowledge about politics that they would have.

I am a 67-year-old Hispanic woman living in Texas. I have some college education but no degree. My family income is between $80,000 and $100,000 a year. In politics, I consider myself a strong Democrat. I would describe my political views as moderate. I never attend religious services. I follow what's going on in government and public affairs hardly at all.

It is November 2026. In this year's midterm U.S. Senate election in Texas, the main candidates are a Republican and a Democrat. I will vote for ...

Reply with exactly one of: Republican, Democrat, Other, Would not vote. No other text.
The wording follows Bisbee et al. (2024): answer as the person, using only what they would know. Every persona is asked five times per model at temperature 1.0, so a persona’s answer is a distribution, not a single vote. Pure independents mostly answer “Other”, so they are asked a second, forced-choice question that allows only the Republican or the main opponent, as in survey follow-ups for undecided voters.




Persona share. For each persona and model, the Republican share is Republican answers divided by answers for any major candidate actually on the ballot (Republican, Democrat or independent). Pure independents use their forced-choice answers.
Weights. Each persona counts as its CES survey weight times its chance of voting: validated turnout for 2024, and turnout rates by age group, college and news interest estimated from CES 2022 for the 2026 midterm.
State estimate. The weighted mean of persona shares, with a bootstrap standard error.




Raw synthetic shares are not forecasts. For each backtested model a line is fitted to the 33 races of 2024 (GPT-4o mini: actual = 0.19 + 0.65 × estimate; Llama 3.3 70B: actual = 0.21 + 0.62 × estimate), which pulls the estimates toward the middle and shifts them toward Republicans. The 2026 estimates are passed through that line. Uncertainty then comes from five sources in 10,000 simulated elections: a national swing shared by all states (standard deviation 3 points, an assumption, because one election cannot measure it), a state-level error (standard deviation 4.7 points, measured by leaving each 2024 race out in turn), the model used, and sampling error in the synthetic voters.

title: 2026 U.S. Senate elections
text:
Synthetic is not a poll. The “voters” are 2024 respondents described to a model; no one answered a 2026 survey.
Calibration rests on one election. The line that corrects the models is fitted to 33 races in 2024, and a midterm may differ.
Some uncertainty is assumed, not measured. The 3-point national swing is a judgement, and the seats-not-up count is taken from the forecast script.
Candidates are described by party, not name. The model cannot know who the nominees are, so the favoured candidate is the nominee of the favoured side.
Independents are the hard part. Models agree with real independents about two thirds of the time in 2024, and four races have an independent challenger.
Models differ in knowledge. The backtested models have older knowledge cutoffs than DeepSeek V4 Flash, which has no backtest.

How independents and special races are coded

Independents who caucus with a party are coded by that party in the certified results: Angus King (Maine) and Bernie Sanders (Vermont) count as Democrats. The CES Senate question already places them in its Democratic slot. Independents who do not caucus with a party (such as Dan Osborn in Nebraska 2024) stay in other.
Special and regular races are treated alike. A race counts if, after that coding, it has both a Democratic and a Republican candidate; a state with two such races in one year (for example Georgia 2020) pools their votes. Nebraska 2024’s regular race (Fischer v. Osborn) has no Democrat, so only its special race (Ricketts v. Love) counts.

text:
Leakage audit
A forecast may only use what was known before the election. I checked every step of the pipeline for information that would not have been available, and fixed what I found.








Issue
What could leak
Fix




Same-year features
Features and targets came from the same survey year and the same respondents; for 2026 we only have 2024 data.
Features are now lagged two years (cycle y uses the survey of y - 2); same-year tables are kept only to measure the leak.


ACS vintage
The ACS 5-year estimate for year Y is published after the year-Y election.

text:
How the headline model was chosen
The headline forecast is not picked by looking at the final results. It is chosen the standard way: by validation performance, then reported on a holdout cycle that played no part in the choice.

Candidates: four feature sets (ces, ces+acs, prior, ces+prior) crossed with three training windows (all earlier cycles, the last two, the last one): 12 models. By project decision the headline trains on all six cycles, so only the four all candidates are eligible to be chosen; the other windows are shown for reference.
Validation: each candidate predicts 2018, 2020 and 2022, trained only on earlier cycles (forward-chaining). The winner among the eligible candidates is the one with the lowest error in the Democratic two-party share against certified results (winner accuracy breaks ties).
Holdout: 2024, the most recent cycle, is predicted by every candidate for transparency but never used to choose.

title: 2026 U.S. Senate elections
text:
Method

Unit of analysis: one row per state per election cycle.
Features (lagged two years): survey-weighted state profile (share male, white, Black, Hispanic, college-educated, mean age, Republican and Democratic party identification), ACS demographics when available, and a midterm-year indicator.
Targets: weighted Democratic, Republican and Undecided/other shares of Senate vote intent, which sum to one. A multi-class regression is fit on additive log-ratios, so predictions stay positive and sum to one.
Penalty: ridge, chosen by leave-one-out cross-validation.
2026 features: no 2026 survey exists, so the 2024 profiles are carried forward.
Candidate characteristics are not modelled. A search found no open dataset covering candidates’ race, gender and incumbency for both major-party Senate candidates across 2014-2024 (the FEC flags incumbency but not race or gender; Ballotpedia and OpenSecrets are not open). The 2026 nominee names, incumbency and portraits on this page are used for display only, not as model inputs.

Run the whole pipeline with uv run scripts/05-regression.py and rebuild the figures with uv run scripts/06-make_figures.py.

title: 2026 U.S. Senate elections
text:
Caveats

Targets are survey intent, not votes; “Undecided” includes Not Sure, No One and third-party answers.
State profiles come from survey samples; small states have few respondents.
Party-identification features come from the same respondents as the targets.
No candidate-level model inputs (race, gender, incumbency, quality, spending; no open dataset) and no uncertainty intervals yet.
Independents who caucus with a party (e.g. Maine, Vermont) are coded by party label.

The full list is in caveats.txt in the repository.
